title: Remark
body_md: It should be emphasised that, in the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:global}, no additional assumption is postulated on $\bm{F}$; the interpretation is that drillstring-wellbore friction, being an intrinsically dissipative phenomenon, is itself non-malign for the well-posedness of the system. Aside from the viscous drag terms, the dominant source of nonlinearity in the PDEs arises indeed from the dependence of the normal force on the drillstring stress, pipe pressure, and annulus pressure, all of which evolve in closed loop with the frictional forces. Consequently, the principal obstacle to well-posedness is not friction itself, but the nonlinear feedback coupling between the generated tangential forces and the state-dependent normal load.

label: remark:GDD
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark:GDD}
Under the additional assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:global}, the coefficients $\phi_{i0}(\overline{\bm{w}}),\phi_{i2}(\overline{\bm{w}}),\phi_{i3}(\overline{\bm{w}}), \phi_{i4}(\overline{\bm{w}}), \phi_{if}(\overline{\bm{w}}) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ become indepndent of $\overline{\bm{w}}$, and the matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f(\overline{\bm{w}}),\bm{\eta},\overline{\bm{w}})$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:MathTheta} reduces to a matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})$, with $\mathbf{\Theta} \in C^0(\mathbb{R}_{> 0}^{16};\mathbf{M}_4(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}))$. In particular, since $\rho(\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta}))<1$, the inverse $(\mathbf{I}_4-\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta}))^{-1}$ exists and is componentwise nonnegative. Therefore, selecting $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^4 \ni \overline{\bm{w}} = c_w (\mathbf{I}_4-\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta}))^{-1} \bm{1}_4 $ for some sufficiently large $c_w\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ gives $(\mathbf{I}_4-\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})) \overline{\bm{w}} = c_w\bm{1}_4$, ensuring that inequality~\eqref{eq:condInitiDHDD} holds trivially. In this way, the estimate~\eqref{eq:BoundedandISSEst} holds for all inputs $\bm{U}\in C^0(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0};\mathbb{R}^{n_U})$ and ICs $(\bm{X}_0,\bm{w}_0) \in C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_X+8})$ satisfying the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:global} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:friction}.

title: Remark
body_md:
In contrast to the well-posedness analysis of Sect.~\ref{sect:wellPos}, which demonstrated that -- for $\od{\theta 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{p}}(z)}{z} \approx 0$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:nomN} -- drillstring-wellbore friction dynamics plays little to no role in determining the well-posedness of the ODE--PDE interconnection~\eqref{eq:ODE--PDEsystem}, Theorem~\ref{thm:Stability} suggests that it might alter its stability, even in the absence of oscillating normal loads. To elucidate this aspect, it is possible to assume $\od{\theta 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{p}}(z)}{z} \approx 0$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:nomN} and consider the matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})$ of Remark~\ref{remark:GDD}, along with the more conservative sufficient condition $\norm{\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})} < 1$ in place of $\rho(\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})) < 1$. Denoting by $\mathbf{M}_{4}(\mathbb{R}) \ni \mathbf{\Theta}_0(\bm{\eta}) \triangleq \mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{0},\bm{\eta})$ the matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}(\bm{\phi}_f,\bm{\eta})$ in the absence of friction, suppose that $\norm{\mathbf{\Theta}_0(\bm{\eta})} < 1$. Then, inspection of Eqs.~\eqref{eq:fsPD} and~\eqref{eq.FS} indicates that the ISS estimate~\eqref{eq:BoundedandISSEst1} is still guaranteed provided that
\begin{align}
\dfrac{C_{f2}\eta_{43}}{\sqrt{2}\rho 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{s}}}(\rho 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{s}}-\rho)\mathrm{g} \sup_{z \in [0,1]}\abs{\sin\theta 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{p}}(z)} < 1-\norm{\mathbf{\Theta}_0(\bm{\eta})}.
\end{align}
Therefore, friction may reduce the available stability margin associated with this sufficient condition. Of course, since the requirements of Theorem~\ref{thm:Stability} are only sufficient, their violation does not imply loss of stability; rather, it merely indicates that this particular criterion is no longer conclusive.

title: Remark
body_md:
The sufficient conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:Stability} also provide useful guidelines for reducing the risk of instability and correctly designing the geometrical configuration of the pipes. Indeed, the coefficients appearing in Eq.~\eqref{coeffs:K} depend on the physical parameters governing the transport velocities, as well as on the pipe geometry through the cross-sectional areas $A 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{p}}(z)$, $A 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{a}}(z)$, and $A 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{b}}(z)$. In particular, Eqs.~\eqref{coeffs:K} and~\eqref{eq:functionsAlpha} show that the interconnection gains can be reduced by avoiding abrupt variations in the cross-sectional areas.

name: Geometrical design

title: Proof
body_md:
The estimate~\eqref{eq:contract} together with~\eqref{€q:contrConst} implies that, for sufficiently small $\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, the mapping $\bm{\Phi} : \mathcal{B}_{\rho}(\bm{Y}_0) \to \mathcal{X}_\delta$ defined as in Eqs.~\eqref{eq:ODE_Phi} and~\eqref{eq:PhiPDEs} is a strict contraction on $\mathcal{B}_{\rho}(\bm{Y}_0)$. By Banach's fixed-point theorem, $\bm{\Phi}(\bm{Y})$ admits a unique fixed point $\bm{Y}=(\bm{X},\widetilde{\bm{w}}) \in C^0([0,\delta];C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_{Y}}))$, which is the unique generalised solution of the transformed system~\eqref{eq:wp_transformed_system}. Since the exponential change of variables~\eqref{eq:esponentialTransf} is an isomorphism of $C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^8)$, the original system~\eqref{eq:ODE--PDEsystem} is also locally well-posed in $C^0([0,\delta];C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_{X}+8})) \cong C^0([0,1]\times[0,\delta];\mathbb{R}^{n_{X}+8})$. Moreover, repeating the procedure above with ICs $\bm{Y}(\cdot,\delta) = (\bm{X}(\cdot,\delta),\widetilde{\bm{w}}(\cdot,\delta)) \in C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_{Y}})$ satisfying the zeroth-order compatibility condition at the initial time $\delta$, a new solution may be obtained on an interval $[\delta,\delta+\eta]$, where $\eta \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ depends only on the IC $\bm{Y}(z,\delta)$. 

\paragraph{Blow-up alternative.}
Let now $t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the maximal existence time of the solution. If $t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}<\infty$, then $\lim_{t\uparrow t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}} \norm{\bm{Y}(\cdot,t)}_{C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_Y})}= \infty$, since otherwise there would exist a sequence $t_n\uparrow t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}$ such that $\norm{\bm{Y}(\cdot,t)}_{C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_Y})} \leq R$ for all $n$ and some $R \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. From the arguments above, this would imply that, for each $t_n$ close enough to $t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}$, the solution $\bm{Y}(z,t)$ obtained on $[0,t_n]$ can be extended on $[0,t_n + \eta]$ with $\eta \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ independent of $t_n$, and $t_n + \eta > t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}$, contradicting its maximality.
Finally, recalling the exponential transformation~\eqref{eq:esponentialTransf}, it may be easily concluded that $\lim_{t\uparrow t 
\ensuremath{_\textnormal{max}}} \norm{\bm{Y}(\cdot,t)}_{C^0([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{n_Y})}= \infty$ is equipollent to Eq.~\eqref{eq:explosion}.
